What makes a square magic?
02

What changes?
What stays the same?

The numbers can move. They can even change. These three operations preserve every declared line sum.

Try a transformation

Rotation and reflection move entries to new positions. Complement replaces each entry x with 26 − x.

All three operations preserve the ordinary magic property. Try one, then follow a line through the new arrangement.

Why the sums survive

Rotation and reflection carry rows, columns, and main diagonals onto other lines in the same set. Under complement, a line of five entries changes from a sum of 65 to 5 × 26 − 65 = 65.

For this particular square, complement gives the same arrangement as a 180° rotation. The operations are conceptually different: one remaps values; the other moves positions.

Square record

Distinct integers 1–25, each used once. Order 5; dimension 2. Ordinary additive line set: five rows, five columns, two main diagonals. All 12 sums are checked against 65 after every transformation. Classical odd-order construction example.
